title: Poland is ditching coal. What happens to its miners?
content: Coal has long been synonymous with Polish energy. Just 20 years ago, 91% of Poland's electricity came from coal. Today, that figure has fallen to around 50%, while wind and solar power account for a quarter of the country's electricity generation. That's a major step forward for a country that started its energy transition from one of the most coal-dependent positions in the EU. Since 2006, Poland’s power-sector emissions have fallen by 30% despite a growing economy and rising electricity demand. That's encouraging news, particularly for southern Poland where some areas have long struggled with poor air quality. One of them is Kraków, my new home. From Kraków – a city that has transformed itself and left much of its smoggy past behind – I travelled north to the Baltic coast, where Poland's energy transition is truly taking off. At the beginning of October, all 76 turbines were installed at Poland's first offshore wind farm. Once fully operational, the wind farm is expected to generate enough electricity to power around 1.5 million homes and meet around 3% of the country's annual electricity demand. title: China isn't laughing at the Mbappé dictator meme
content: Having a bad week? Kylian Mbappé might be having a worse one. On Monday, the French football star lost the Ballon d’Or, football's most prestigious individual award, to England's Harry Kane. And before he'd even had time to get over that, he's now in trouble with an entire country: China. It all started when a short clip from a French interview, aired six months ago, suddenly went viral at the start of the week. Asked about his favourite meme featuring himself, Mbappé said: “The one that made me laugh the most was the video where they put my face on some guy – I think he's a Chinese dictator.” For context, Mbappé has long been the subject of “dictator” jokes online. Fans like to poke fun at his supposedly outsized influence on and off the pitch by comparing him to authoritarian leaders. Even his teammates have joined in: French player Ousmane Dembélé has been heard calling him “Mobut” – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the former dictator of Zaire. But this time, the meme Mbappé was referring to (first posted in 2023, here is the original) wasn’t about just any dictator. title: Too violent for a war? Perfect for a protest!
content: First, I teared up. Then my nose started itching, and then came the coughs. First from those around me, until I joined the choir myself. The crowd grew uneasy, people looked for a way out, and the chaos began. That's how I experienced tear gas for the first time at a protest in Türkiye in 2025, but it could just as easily describe one of the many protests this month where police used tear gas: be it in Belgium, Italy, Albania, or, most importantly, France. Nowhere has tear gas been used more than in France, the country that gave birth to it. According to data from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, analysed by The European Correspondent, some 1,520 protests between 2020 and 2026 involved tear gas. More than half of these took place in France. As common as tear gas remains, it's also widely misunderstood. Tear gas isn't gas Remember this for your next police-violence pub quiz. title: Raving, reading, and resisting in Ukraine
content: It could be Berlin or New York. One autumn evening, hundreds gather in the rounded hall of a brutalist building at Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. A DJ plays soft electronic music. Some drink coffee, others sit on the floor with a book. Nobody is dancing. They call it a book rave. Bring a book and read together. Sit with your friends and talk about books. Go to some of the classes and listen to a lecture about literature. Or simply listen to music and meditate. But in Ukraine, books have become more than a pastime. Over the summer, Russian strikes destroyed an estimated 13 million of them. In Kharkiv, a single drone attack burned eight million books at a publisher's warehouse, including school textbooks and children's stories. “Why attack books?” asks Svitlana, one of the book rave's organisers. To her, the destruction recalls the long history of Russian attempts to suppress Ukrainian culture, from imperial language restrictions to Soviet censorship and executions. In 1937, dozens of Ukrainian writers and artists were murdered in Stalin's purges. title: Loans don't grow on trees
content: Ever wondered what tobacco and banks have in common? Very soon, both will be warning consumers about the risks associated with their products. From 20 November, under new EU rules, adverts for consumer credit will have to include a clear and prominent warning: “Caution! Borrowing money costs money.” Very similar to the ones you see on cigarette packets. The requirement to warn consumers that loans don't grow on trees is part of new regulation to protect EU consumers taking out loans. Lenders will also face stricter requirements on the information they provide in credit adverts. This includes the total cost of borrowing and, where applicable, the loan's duration and repayment instalments. Misleading advertising will also be prohibited. The updated rules extend consumer credit protections to small loans of less than €200 and “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) schemes, which have become increasingly common in online shopping. There is one exception, though: shops that offer interest-free credit directly, without involving a third-party such as Klarna, as long as the purchase is repaid within 50 days. title: How to shut down half a country in 10 days
content: Walking down the aisle of your local supermarket, and all you see are bare shelves and rows of empty boxes. A sign reads: “Delivery not received. Sorry for the inconvenience.” There is no bread, fruit, or vegetables – just frozen food, which you quickly stock up on. This is not a flashback to 2020, when panic-buying for pasta and toilet paper during the Covid-19 pandemic left supermarket shelves emptied. This time, the shortages are linked to workers' protests in southern Italy over soaring fuel prices. It all began with the farmers on 10 October: they called for mass demonstrations in the Italian regions of Calabria, Apulia, Basilicata, and Sicily, and workers in the transport sector immediately joined. Striking hauliers switched off their engines on roads and motorways, and refused to unload their goods. Fishermen also joined the protests, leaving their boats docked at port. The protesters' message is clear: running a farm, a transport or fishing business has become too expensive. Fuel is one major cost, but it's far from being the only one. title: Less friendly with the rest of the world
content: European national football teams play fewer friendlies against non-European opponents than they used to. The number of friendly games played between a UEFA national team and a team from a different confederation dropped from an average of 55.3 games a year before 2019 to 38.6 after 2019. The drop coincides with the launch of the UEFA Nations League in late 2018. This new competition would replace many of the international friendlies teams used to play. UEFA said the aim was to add “status and appeal to national team football.” The number of intercontinental friendlies varies from year to year. It tends to rise in World Cup years, when teams seek opponents from other continents to prepare for the tournament. The number of friendlies rose in 2026, when 43 of the year’s 67 friendlies against non-European teams were played in June, just before the expanded World Cup kicked off.

title: Babe, wake up, press freedom is in danger!
content: What happened: The Czech right-wing populist government, led by billionaire prime minister Andrej Babiš, wants to fundamentally change the country's public media, trying to abolish the licence fee paid directly by citizens and instead fund Czech TV and radio from the state budget. Babiš's government pushed its proposal through a first reading in parliament in a rather shady way. They fast-tracked the parliamentary debate and scheduled the first round of voting at 4.36 in the morning on Saturday last week. Not exactly a common procedure for voting on something this big. It's almost... hmm... as if they tried to get away with something without much public attention. When word spread, spontaneous protest filled the square next to the parliament building throughout the night. The government majority passed the proposal anyway. In 2025, Babiš's ANO party campaigned on the reform, arguing that abolishing licence fees, which currently amount to CZK 205, or €8 per month, would relieve citizens. title: Serbia is free
content: For most of my life, Serbia was a place that you'd better leave. And so I did. But last night, as I followed election results deep into the night all the way from the Netherlands, I felt that Serbia might be a place to come back to for perhaps the first time in my life. Around 21.30 on election night, former president Aleksandar Vučić conceded that his party SNS, which has been in power for the last 14 years, had lost to the Student List, born out of a protest movement that has shaken Serbia since November 2024. Almost instantly, “Serbia is free” echoed all over social media as city streets erupted in joy and celebration. The police, who had been blocking the street in front of the Republic Electoral Commission and patrolling Belgrade since the morning, began to retreat, and two years of building tension was released in fireworks, chants, and dancing deep into the night. The Student List won by a landslide. According to the Republic Electoral Commission, and based on 97% of counted votes, the Student List won 52.65% of the votes and is projected to gain 140 out of 250 parliamentary seats, enough for a parliamentary majority. title: The Black Sea is turning green, and not the good kind
content: “This summer, we went 38 km deep in the Black Sea. You can see how it is more green,” Martin Tomov, a campaigner for Greenpeace Bulgaria, told us. Satellite images from EUMETSAT confirm his observation. The scientific name for this is eutrophication: an excess of nutrients allows algae to bloom, turning rivers and seas from crystal blue to green. It happens when manure or nitrate- and phosphate-based fertilisers spread on farmland run off into rivers. When the algae later die and rot, they strip the water of oxygen, which suffocates fish, and can also release a poisonous gas. “They also block sunlight; it prevents many organisms from surviving, which impacts the entire food chain,” Tomov told us. In 2016, a jogger died on a beach in Brittany, France, after inhaling poisonous gas from rotten algae. A court held the state liable nine years later, and France compensated his family. But Europe is far from responding adequately. Nearly one third of the EU's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters, and 81% of marine waters, are eutrophic according to an EU report from early this year. title: I See You, ICC
content: The International Criminal Court (ICC) won the EU's human rights prize last week, a big vote of support from the European Parliament for its work in putting war criminals on trial and just 13 days after the US imposed sanctions on the tribunal. But it's “somewhat problematic” for the EU's assembly to award the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought to the court “whilst simultaneously being indecisive and arguably weak regarding its responses to the US sanctions,” said Benjamin Thorne, an assistant law professor at the University of Reading. The Hague-based court, backed by 125 countries, has convicted 15 people to date, all from African countries. It currently has arrest warrants for Russian president Vladimir Putin and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Until their deaths, it also was planning or had issued warrants for three Hamas leaders. US secretary of state Marco Rubio earlier this month called the ICC a “rogue court” that might prosecute American soldiers, border patrol agents, or elected leaders. title: Man up, don't save the planet
content: Are you a man who cares about the climate? Then you might be a “soy boy” (or for our less chronically online readers: lacking masculine traits). Research suggests that men who want to protect the environment are often seen as warmer and more caring – traits traditionally associated with femininity. Michael Haselhuhn, an associate professor of management at the University of California, published research on this. When asked if they would use cold water for laundry to save money, most men said they would. “When I said it helps the environment because it saves electricity, the support dropped by 10%,” Haselhuhn said. Across most European countries, there is a gender gap in how women and men see environmental issues. Women tend to care more about protecting the environment than men. “In Northern and Western Europe, men are less likely to vote for green parties or parties that emphasise protecting the environment,” said Ingvild Zinober, a researcher studying the green gender gap at the European University Institute. title: Coffeemaxxed lifestyle
content: As a coffee addict, I dream of living in a city where cafés stay open for as much of the day as possible, ideally opening early and closing late. But my past geographical choices haven’t exactly served me well. To find out where I should have settled, I collected Google Maps listings for cafés in about 80 of Europe’s largest cities, covering roughly 15,000 active cafés. The data revealed a few interesting things beyond opening hours. London and Istanbul have the most café listings, but neither scores particularly well in customer reviews. If you’re after the best-rated cafés, Romania is a good choice: Bucharest’s cafés have a median rating of 4.8 out of 5, based on more than 30,000 reviews. Still, Bucharest wouldn’t satisfy me: its cafés stay open for about 10 hours a day. That’s much better than Leeds, where cafés are open for just seven hours on average. For a coffee fanatic like me, the Balkans and Istanbul may be the best bet: cafés in Tirana, Podgorica, Zagreb and Pristina stay open for around 15 hours a day. title: Extremists have no idea what Norse mythology is really about
content: Thor, the Norse god of thunder, once visited the giant Utgard-Loki. The giant challenged him to empty a drinking horn, lift a cat, and wrestle an old woman. He failed all three and left questioning his power. As it turned out, Utgard-Loki had used magic to hide Thor's real opponents. He had been drinking from the ocean, and the cat was Jörmungandr, the gigantic sea serpent encircling the earth. The old lady? Old age itself. This is the Norse myth I remember most clearly. For most people across Scandinavia and Iceland, the old myths don’t play a big role in everyday life, but there are subtle signs of them. Weekdays, streets, and people are named after Norse gods, for instance. Or the countless TV shows, comics, books, and music inspired by old gods and myths. We don't know when and how Norse mythology started, but it was definitely practised in Scandinavia and Iceland in the late Iron Age (from 500 AD) and Viking Age (800-1050 AD). Northern Europe was then gradually Christianised around the year 1000, through missionaries and due to pressure from foreign trade from the south. title: What does the C say about your yoghurt?
content: Let's say you're in a shop looking for yoghurt. You're standing at the fridge, choosing between strawberry and plain. The pots show five letters, running from a dark-green A to a red E. The one you're holding has a C. Hmmm. Those letters are the Nutri-Score, a label weighing sugars, saturated fat, salt, and calories against fibre, protein, and the content of fruit, vegetables and legumes in products per 100 g or 100 ml. The label was first adopted in France in 2017 and has since been picked up in Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and Spain. International supermarkets have also brought it elsewhere, which is why you'll see the label on Lidl shelves in Latvia, for example. Using it is voluntary for producers. We analysed nearly one million EU-listed packaged products with a Nutri-Score in the Open Food Facts database from all over Europe, and found that nearly three-quarters (73.9%) were rated C, D, or E. title: Your home is their asset
content: Let’s be realistic, housing has always been a business. What has changed however, is its scale. By the end of 2024, the value of global real estate had reached 393 trillion USD (€379 trillion) according to Savills Research real estate analysis. Most of this value came from residential property. This is more than the combined value of all global stocks and debt, and 20 times the value of all the gold ever mined. The market is not driven by what Barbara Steenbergen, the EU representative of the International Union of Tenants (IUT), calls “small amateur landlords”, but by large investment and pension funds. These funds are often registered in one country but source capital globally, Manuel Aalbers, professor of human geography at KU Leuven, told The European Correspondent (TEC). “They might have Spanish or German names, yet the money they invest comes from the City of London or Wall Street.” Listed real estate funds, which account for only a fraction of the market, owned €199 billion worth of property in the EU in 2024, up from just €5 billion in 2004. title: Serbian students are threatening Vučić's long rule
content: When 16 people died after the concrete canopy above the entrance to the train station in Novi Sad (Serbia's second-biggest city) collapsed in November 2024, few could imagine what would follow: two years of mass protests that grew into the largest student protest movement since the fall of Milošević in 2000. More than 2,400 demonstrations took place in the first year alone, including the largest protest in the country's history on 15 March 2025. After two years of pressure, president Aleksandar Vučić called early parliamentary elections in early September. He faces unprecedented mobilisation both in Serbia and among the Serbian diaspora. Protests in support of the movement have taken place around the world, while more than 102,000 people living abroad have registered to vote – more than double the number registered in the 2023 elections. title: Giving Amsterdam's streets a face
content: If you live in a European city, it's likely your street is named after someone. But do you know who that person was, what they did to earn a place on the map, or what they looked like? In Amsterdam, finding out might be a little easier. Many streets, squares, and bridges feature information panels with a portrait and a short biography of the historical figure they are named after. And all this thanks to a grassroots initiative run by two Amsterdam residents. Geef straten een gezicht (“Give streets a face”) is a project launched by photographer and graphic designer Paul Fennis in 2013. He installs portraits and short biographies to help people understand the history behind their street names. Since 2020, journalist and writer Shirley Brandeis has worked with him on the project. “It started as a one-off thing,” Brandeis told The European Correspondent. Fennis lived on a square named after J. J. Cremer, a Dutch writer who campaigned against child labour. He often saw children from a nearby school playing there and thought they should know about him. title: Playing by the rules?
content: The strength of courts, rights and checks on power is declining across Europe, reflecting a broader global recession, according to data from the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index. The index measures eight factors, including checks on government power, the absence of corruption and the justice system. Since 2021, Europe's average score has fallen in seven of the eight areas, and remained unchanged in one: corruption. Although the declines are small, less than 1.5 points out of 100, they are consistent. Two-thirds of European countries scored lower in 2026 than in 2021. Russia, Belarus, Türkiye and Serbia remain at the bottom of the European rankings, but some of the steepest declines were also recorded in Georgia, Portugal and Slovakia. Europe still scores substantially higher than the global average, and nine of the world's ten highest-ranked countries are European.

title: How to win (and lose) an ally in 10 days
content: These past few weeks mark a more deliberate and open campaign of coercion against Europe and Ukraine by the US and Russia. Both US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin have something to gain: a better result for the Republicans in the upcoming US midterm elections, a Ukraine pushed into defeat, and a Europe that still depends on the US. What happened: 9 October: Trump and Putin hold a long phone call. Afterwards, the US lifts sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027, letting Russia sell millions of tonnes of it to the US and global markets. Historian Anne Applebaum called it “an abrupt, Hail Mary attempt to force Ukraine to surrender and to save the Russian economy.” Never mind that, according to the EU's economy chief, Russia can't export enough diesel to change prices. On the call, Putin proposes a summit with Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping in China next month to decide Ukraine's future, without Ukraine. According to a Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter, Putin wants a “second Yalta”, the 1945 conference where the US, UK, and Soviet Union carved up Europe, this time with the US, Russia, and China dividing the world between them.

title: Good news, the robots trying to take your job are bad at it
content: A supermarket on the outskirts of Copenhagen has become the unlikely site of a futuristic labour experiment. Føtex is training humanoid robots to restock its shelves at night, a task it estimates currently takes 40-50% of its staff's time. One day, they hope to have two high-tech assistants in every store, not to replace employees but to speed up routine tasks, they say. But for now, the robots aren't exactly autonomous – trainers from the Danish start-up HIVE Robots still guide their every movement using VR goggles. Nor are they... good. Still much slower than humans, they're meant to improve as they accumulate and process data over time. Despite their awesome looks, even the most advanced humanoid robots have had some spectacular public mishaps recently, including face-planting during demonstrations. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report estimated the top AI robotic systems could only complete 12% of household tasks when tested in realistic simulations. Part of the problem is hardware: rigid joints, tough materials, and limited sensors make movements stiff. title: Priced out of Netflix
content: When Netflix raised my subscription price again to €17 per month, I paid and moved on. But it made me wonder what the same subscription costs everyone else. Netflix charges different prices in different countries, depending on local purchasing power. After all, not everyone can afford the €25 a month the Swiss pay. I found that Netflix's lower pricing in poorer countries is still far smaller than the gap in wages to richer countries. So while the average Dane earns their monthly subscription in the time it takes to watch an episode of Friends, the average Ukrainian has to work through the whole of Pulp Fiction.

title: Do we really need all this cheese water?
content: A spoonful of whey in your morning cereal, a protein shake after an intense leg session. For many of us, focusing on protein in our diets has become a habit. Fewer of us know where the protein taking over our supermarkets actually comes from. Gym-goers' favourite product, whey powder, is a by-product of cheesemaking: it starts as the yellowish liquid left over after milk is thickened into curds and strained. That liquid is then dried into powder. Whey keeps most of milk’s lactose and water-soluble vitamins and about a fifth of its protein. For centuries, people drank it (for example the Scottish whey wine called “blaand“) or used it as a medicine for gut health. Today, up to 200 million tonnes of whey are produced as a by-product of industrial cheesemaking globally. The European Union alone makes more than a quarter of it. The hype around high-protein food has increased demand for whey, but production volumes have stayed the same, as they're linked to cheese production. As a result, the price of whey has skyrocketed in Europe in recent months. title: Elected women never asked to be nudified, yet here we are
content: As a person of a marginalised gender, existing online means being constantly amazed by all the ways the internet can be used against you, no matter how powerful you are. One of the latest additions to that arsenal are “nudification” apps, AI-powered tools that can be prompted to create fake, sexually explicit pictures and videos of people, usually without their consent. All you need is a single photo of them. Two recent reports by Berlin thinktank Agora Digitale Transformation looked at how these tools are affecting politicians. The first one found 147 members of national European parliaments were either directly depicted in fake nudes or listed on sites that help people create them. Unsurprisingly, women were far more likely to be affected than men – 33 times more likely, in fact. Surprisingly, political affiliation hardly affected who was targeted, but seniority did. People in more prominent positions were more likely to be affected. title: We brought back the lynx, but will we save the rest?
content: When Portuguese biologist Henrique Pereira was a kid in the 1980s, there were almost no vultures left in southern Europe. Wildlife that was once close to extinction made a comeback. Sabien Leemans, biodiversity manager at WWF EU, noted that “in Europe, industrial development started way before 1970. title: Your fries are getting shorter (but no less crispy)
content: No matter what the weather did to this year's harvest, Belgium will still deliver its biggest contribution to the culinary cultural canon: fries. They will still taste good. But this season, the long ones may be missing from your paper cone. First came the potato glut. Last year’s harvest was so abundant that potatoes sold without a contract went for between €0 and €5 per 100 kg – far below production costs, said Daniel Ryckmans, an agronomist at the Walloon potato organisation FIWAP. For this season, the sector asked farmers to plant less, and they did: Belgium's potato fields shrank by 17.4%. Then the summer came, and multiple extreme heatwaves came with it. “This year there was not enough rain. And above that, it was too hot,” Ryckmans told us. The result of this combination is fewer, smaller potatoes. A September assessment by the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU), a non-profit organisation based in the UK, put Belgian yields 21% below their five-year average. title: European businesses are keen to go green
content: The EU has a favourite word: competitiveness. To better compete in the global economy, the European Commission is rewriting (and often weakening) environmental rules for businesses, for example to reduce reporting burdens. Making life easier for our biggest industries sounds reasonable: we shouldn't impose rules that drive them out of business, should we? Yet what do businesses actually want? A recent GlobeScan survey commissioned by the environmental group WWF asked 350 European business leaders. Only 29% said the EU's environmental simplification efforts have helped them, while 55% reported a negative or mixed impact. Meanwhile, 91% said shifting to a low-carbon economy will make Europe more competitive in the long run. Some of that frustration comes from companies that moved towards sustainability first. Many invested in line with the Commission's own green rules, and now feel punished by the uncertainty of changing rules. title: Stamps worth more than your house
content: If you've never thought long and hard about stamps, you are most certainly not a philatelist – a student or collector of postage history. During the stamp craze of the mid-19th century, the French spoke about “timbromanie”, or the mania of rabid philatelist collectors. Who would've thought that humble postage stickers would unleash such heated passion among Europe's well-to-do? The most valuable stamps in the world are mostly the freaks among them, including those printed in the wrong colour or displaying their subject upside down. Others are famous for their lore, like the improvised “1856 British Guiana 1-Cent Magenta” (the second stamp in the visual), printed by British colonists after the Crown failed to send them a new batch in time. As such, stamps have always been as much about power as they are about mail. Colonial and imperial rulers used them to thrust their faces into the daily lives of people; Poland and Czechoslovakia, once independent, reissued stamps from elsewhere by printing right over them.

Known as the Amazon of Europe for the scale of its wilderness, the reserve stretches across some of the continent's most valuable river landscapes. Sadiković was pointing at sandbanks that are usually underwater. After a hot, dry summer, water levels in the Drava river had fallen to record lows. The exposed banks had been in the sun so long that grass and shrubs were beginning to grow. “I've never experienced such conditions,” said Sadiković, “and I was born on the banks of the river.” Indeed, his hometown Osijek has a maternity ward that overlooks the river, and the extroverted Croatian has spent most of his 52 years living alongside it, swimming and fishing in its waters. title: Europeans win, abroad
content: When Belgian physicist Francis Halzen was awarded this year’s Nobel prize in Physics, he became the ninth European among the past 10 physics laureates. But Halzen, who won his prize while working at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, is also part of a less celebrated trend. Four of those nine Europeans carried out the research that earned them the prize outside their home countries, mostly in the United States. The trend runs across all scientific Nobel categories (physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, and economics), where European laureates are increasingly likely to have done their prize-winning work abroad. It is most pronounced in economics, where more than two-thirds of European winners did their Nobel-recognised research at a foreign university. In physics and chemistry, the share is more than a third. The Nobel prize reflects a wider brain drain with European researchers leaving for better-funded positions elsewhere. The EU is trying to bring dissatisfied or laid-off American researchers to Europe through its “Choose Europe for Science” initiative. content: Protesters are still waving pink flamingos on wooden poles, over four months into their movement. As they march through the streets in central Albania they chant ”Rama in jail, Berisha in jail,” referring to the prime minister and the opposition leader. title: Want to ditch your gas boiler? Ask your city
content: You may never have worried about the Strait of Hormuz, had it not been for the impact on your wallet, right? With gas prices hitting record highs and fossil fuels contributing to climate change, perhaps it's finally time to say goodbye to the old gas boiler in the bathroom? Hmmm... What seems like an easy choice on paper can be a much harder one in practice. Whether we can make the switch, and when, depends on the alternatives available where we live, how much money we need to invest and whether public support is available to help us go greener. Your local government has a big influence on all three. Local politicians can make practical decisions about heat networks and building renovation. They are also closer to residents, which makes them best equipped to identify people affected by energy poverty and target support where it is needed most. That's precisely what Greenpeace decided to track: they followed 15 European cities and assessed how well they're doing in the green heating race (or whether they are racing backwards). content: France, Belgium, Spain, Albania – young people have taken to the streets across Europe in recent weeks. Their grievances are different – school conditions, housing, or corrupt governments. title: EU governments are sweating over trade with China
content: For years, China has been selling far more to EU customers than it buys in return. The EU imported nearly €54 billion worth of goods in July, while exporting only €17.4 billion. That's a difference of €36.5 billion, or more than €1 billion a day flowing from EU countries to China. Over the past decade, that deficit has more than doubled in value as the EU keeps buying more from China, increasingly higher-value goods. European manufacturers and retailers complain that they can no longer compete with Chinese rivals who sell their products for far less, partly thanks to government subsidies that help cover their costs. Lower exports and sales of EU goods hurt the EU economy and can put EU companies out of business. title: Will tiny viruses rescue us?
content: You can’t see them, but bacteriophages are on your skin, in wastewater, and in the depths of our oceans. Wherever there are bacteria, there are bacteriophages – or phages, for short. He researches phages and is – in his own words – a “phage enthusiast”. Phage research is having a revival as an increasingly promising way to tackle multi-drug resistant (MDR) infections as bacteria become more resistant to antibiotics. Despite being discovered in 1917, eleven years before antibiotics, phage therapy is still considered experimental due to a lack of randomised clinical trials. So what can we expect? title: When food becomes too political
content: Good news for Asterix fans: the banquet is making a comeback in rural France. title: In Amsterdam, you can ring a doorbell to test your drugs
content: After meeting his dealer, Peter (not his real name) hunts for a doorbell in one of Amsterdam's narrow alleys. “Drug service”, reads the label underneath the button. “I'm here to test some drugs,” Peter says into the intercom, and the door opens. Inside, a few people wait silently on plastic chairs, and leaflets are scattered across a table. About 20 minutes later, it's Peter's turn. He gets called to a different room to test his cocaine. Peter has walked into one of the paradoxes of Dutch drug policy: buying and possessing drugs such as cocaine is illegal, yet testing them is allowed as part of a government-supported system. A network of 34 locations has been checking drugs across the country for over 30 years. It's a similar construction to the famous Dutch weed policy: possessing cannabis is technically illegal but “gedoogd” (tolerated) in many cases. The testing locations follow the Dutch policy that completely stopping drug use is impossible, and that adding measures to reduce harm, besides prevention, is beneficial to protect public health. title: Spare some change for the EU?
content: The EU had a budget of just under €150 billion to spend last year, less than Denmark's. This covered payouts to farmers and researchers, humanitarian aid, and salaries for its civil servants. Around two-thirds of that money comes from EU member state governments, who contribute based on the size of their economies. But the EU also raises some of its own income, or “own resources”, which includes a small slice of the value-added tax (VAT) on what we buy, a levy on plastic waste, and part of the customs duties on imports. title: When missiles strike, Ukrainians turn to their phones
content: A first missile hits. Then a second, then a third. The walls shake and car alarms, triggered by the blasts, mix with the sound of air raid sirens outside. title: What does eating seasonally even mean?
content: Let me take you into my mother’s basement. Past a heavy door that keeps out summer heat and winter frost, down the stairs, is a dimly lit room full of earthy smells and treasure. The shelves are lined with jars in every shade, from bright green to aubergine: jams, kompots, courgette, tomato and cabbage salads, fermented and pickled cucumbers, alongside berry and apple juice and whatever else my mother has decided to experiment with. There are also boxes of potatoes, carrots, beetroot and apples. Everything here comes from the garden above. This is the old-school way of eating seasonally in the Baltics: eating food fresh while it grows, and preserving it for when it doesn't – in winter. But a supermarket in Rīga sells fresh strawberries and tomatoes all year round. title: Please join the EU, but behave!
content: Joining the EU is a long, hard trek for would-be members. Montenegro, which is closest to joining, has been negotiating for more than a decade. Now, the EU wants to update its terms and conditions for new members. If a country misbehaves, it could lose its funding or even its vote on EU decisions. Harsh words. Their real audience seems to be the EU's existing members, who need convincing that enlarging the club is a good idea after 16 years of Viktor Orbán's Hungary thumbing its nose at EU laws and values. The EU has been slow to fix a date for any of them to join. title: 12 Europeans walk into Oktoberfest
content: It’s 15.25 outside the Schottenhamel Festzelt, the oldest Oktoberfest beer tent in Munich, with space for around 9,000 people. A small crowd of women in dirndls (traditional Alpine dresses) of varying sleeve-puffiness and neckline depth, and men in assorted shades of brown leather shorts, is getting shifty. Oktoberfest, or Wiesn as the locals call it, is the world's biggest folk festival. Abroad, it's the quintessential German tradition, but most Germans will point out it's mostly Bavarians celebrating Bavaria. I'm here with 11 other 20-somethings from around Europe, and we've all dressed the part. The sleeve-puffiness of my own dirndl is off the charts. I feel like a 19th-century milkmaid. 16.27 We're among the lucky ones: we have a table and benches from which to drink beer by the litre from “Maß” jugs at €15.80 each. “Oktoberfest is about coming together,” Annika, 25, from Munich, yells over the sound of the live band. “I’ve been going since I was 14. All my friends who left the city come back this time of the year. You walk through the tent and see people you know, and you just hug them.” This year cracked the all-time record of Oktoberfest visitors in Munich at 7.4 million.

title: The fungal networks hiding beneath our feet
content: Something massive is hiding underground: large networks of tiny threads, each many times thinner than a hair. If laid out end to end, they would stretch about 110 quadrillion kilometres – roughly 730 million times the distance from Earth to the sun. These tiny threads are fungi, specifically mycorrhizal fungi. You may think of fungi as mushrooms, but these ones live mostly underground. “Underneath your foot, you might have hundreds of metres of these fungal threads,” Justin Stewart, an evolutionary ecologist and postdoctoral fellow at the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), told us. Stewart is the lead author of a recent study published in Science, used by SPUN to create the first-ever global map of mycorrhizal fungi. These fungi are fantastic biological partners to plants. They partner up with more than 70% of land-based plant species, trading nutrients they get from the soil for plant sugars. “These networks are basically one of Earth’s circulatory systems,” said Toby Kiers, executive director of SPUN and evolutionary biologist at the Free University of Amsterdam. title: Never been to a protest? You'll still feel the crackdown
content: Civic space is one of those things you won't notice until it's gone. The United Nations defines it as “the environment that enables people and groups to participate meaningfully in the political, economic, social and cultural life of their societies.” Measuring civic space is as much about laws as it is about vibes: besides the legal rights guaranteeing free speech, freedom of assembly, protest, or protection from hate speech, it's also about feeling at ease in exercising these rights – like going to a protest without a mask in case there's tear gas, or an umbrella in case there's a water cannon. Put simply: civic space is crucial to our democracies. But it's never fully stable, and nothing in the past few years has made that clearer than the restrictions on Palestine solidarity protests. title: What happened to EU sanctions on Israel? (The sequel)
content: The EU promised to sanction Israeli ministers and partially suspend the EU-Israel trade agreement in September 2025. Neither has happened. Why? Shortly after European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen made those promises, Donald Trump announced a ceasefire in Gaza, and the EU largely shelved its sanctions plans. title: The housing crisis just ended the Spanish government
content: What happened: Less than two weeks ago, Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from the flat in Madrid she had lived in for over 70 years, after the building’s new owner, a real estate company called Urbagestión, raised her rent from €500 to €2,650. Her case sparked outrage over the situation in Spain’s housing market, where even a couple with wages well above the average cannot afford to buy or rent a place on their own. Mass protests across the country pressured prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s government to issue two decrees to prevent cases such as Maricarmen’s, by limiting rent increases and banning real estate companies from buying more flats, among other things. Both failed to secure sufficient support in parliament and were rejected last Friday. On Monday, Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November. “We have had to contend with very powerful economic and social elites who do not stand for election,” Sánchez said, indirectly referring to alleged lobbying efforts by real estate companies to have the decrees repealed. title: Taxing wealth can be expensive
content: “Tax the rich” is a rallying cry for some to raise government revenue, but the Netherlands actually loses money on its household capital income tax. Governments tax the money a household makes from what it owns – its capital income, which includes returns on savings and investments, and rental income, among other things. Some countries, like France and Luxembourg, raise a relatively high portion (4.5%) of their tax revenue this way. Others, like Slovakia (0.4%) and Malta (0.3%), rely less heavily on taxing household capital to fill their treasury. The Netherlands (-0.9%) breaks the scale by giving away more tax breaks for homeowners than it collects via household capital income tax. That tax relief increases people's borrowing capacity for a mortgage, leading to higher housing prices. As a result, renters end up effectively subsidising homeowners: all taxpayers, regardless of whether they own capital or a home themselves, help fill the gap left by this scheme.

title: French teens are taking on the state
content: A burning building, charging police officers and witty slogans disappearing in a haze of tear gas: high schoolers are protesting all over France. Mass demonstrations have taken place all week. What's going on? On 21 September, teachers at a high school in the Paris suburbs went on strike to protest working conditions. Their students blocked their school to support them, and several other schools in the area followed suit. It eventually spread to other parts of the country. By 4 October, over 5,000 students had been arrested, most of them under 18, since the start of the protests. Hundreds of schools had to close down after a few days, with students attending classes from home. Nearly 200 were injured after riot police were deployed, according to Monday's estimates by the minister of education. For striking students, the protest is a fight to get the education they were always promised but never given. That starts with getting the right number of teachers. In September, 53% of French secondary and high schools started the year short of at least one teacher, according to the country's leading union. Just over 7% of teaching hours could not take place in 2025 due to absent teachers.

title: Can you game the climate crisis away?
content: Of course not. But you might be able to get more people to care about it. Pablo and his team developed the game, which you can play on your laptop or smartphone. The goal is to stop bulldozers from tearing down trees. The catch is that you can never win: there are only a few people defending the square against an endless stream of bulldozers. With every tree that falls, the temperature in the square rises. At the end, all that remains is an empty concrete rectangle under a scorching 42°C, alongside a message inviting players to join the committee fighting to save Piazza della Libertà in Monterotondo, a small town near Rome, Italy. “We wanted to engage people in this cause, make sure they are aware and informed about what's going on,” Pablo, the committee's spokesperson, told us. title: Is the sky the limit?
content: “Fewer planes, more life,” read one of the banners carried by protesters in Barcelona a couple of weeks ago. Together with demonstrators in the Balearic Islands, they were opposing airport expansions that would bring even more tourists to already overcrowded places. Four of the 12 airports that Spanish operator Aena plans to expand – including Barcelona airport – already account for 66% of the country’s CO₂ emissions from departing flights, according to a report by Transport and Environment (T&E), a clean transport NGO. The report states that aviation emissions in Spain had risen above pre-pandemic levels by 2025, the fastest increase among European markets. T&E analysed plans to expand 20 airports across 10 European countries. Together, the projects would add 225 million tonnes of CO₂ to current emissions – roughly equivalent to Spain's annual emissions – complicating Europe's efforts to reach carbon neutrality by 2050. title: Forever chemicals are in our blood
content: “Cognitive dissonance” is when you hold two conflicting views. Or keep doing something even though you know it conflicts with your beliefs. It's not really a surprise to me that there's chemical pollution around me. I can smell car fumes and see plastic lying in the grass on my way to work. Local ponds and streams are often choked with algae in a region struggling with excess nitrate from agricultural fertilisers. But do I shun plastic? Only buy organic food? Ensure there are absolutely no potentially problematic chemicals in my home? Nope. It's easier to do nothing when you don't really know what you're facing. But that wilful blindness had to end when the European Parliament's Green-EFA group asked me to be one of 110 volunteers from nine countries to get our blood tested for PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. title: Young women and men are drifting apart politically
content: A trend is gripping many of Europe's democracies: young men are increasingly voting for right-wing parties, while young women are moving further left. In Sweden's September election, 22% of men aged 18 to 30 voted for the far-right Sweden Democrats, compared with half as many women. Young women, meanwhile, vote much further left. In Berlin's recent state election, which was won by the left party, just over half of women under 25 voted for the party, compared to 34% of men. In Poland, the gap is especially stark: 26.3% of men aged 18 to 29 voted for the far-right Confederation party in 2023. title: Winter is coming, are we ready?
content: As temperatures across Europe begin to fall back into the single digits, the region is facing an unenviable challenge: how to get through the colder months with gas reserves at record lows and prices at record highs? EU-wide gas storage was about 70% full in late September – the lowest level recorded in the EU in at least fifteen years for this time of year. This is a result of tighter global liquified natural gas (LNG) supplies amid the US-Israel war on Iran, as well as the EU's decision to relax its gas storage targets last year. The rules were originally introduced in response to the 2022 energy crisis – following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The demand for gas-generated electricity was also higher than usual this summer as extreme heatwaves forced some power plants to reduce or suspend operations. While solar power helped meet the surge in daytime electricity demand from air conditioning, gas was relied upon more heavily in the evenings, explained Chris Rosslowe, energy analyst at the energy think tank Ember. title: Drink a cup of coffee and I'll tell you your future
content: Today is International Coffee Day, so we have to ask: is there a more European drink than coffee? Europeans drink more coffee per capita than anywhere else in the world, on average. And across the continent, coffee has taken on countless forms – from the Italian cappuccino and Irish coffee, to the Greek frappé. But coffee in Europe is about more than what we put in the cup. title: Getting back with the ex?
content: What happened: The UK could think about getting back together with the EU after a bad decade since the break-up, British prime minister Andy Burnham told BBC radio on Wednesday. It's just one of several “options that need to be considered,” he said. Why it matters: None of the six (!) other British leaders since the 2016 vote to leave the EU have seriously mentioned rejoining the bloc. Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer had promised to rebuild relations with the EU, the country's largest trading partner. But his and Burnham's Labour party had “red lines” that forbade a return to the EU's single market, freedom of movement, or even an alternative arrangement, like the customs union which allows Türkiye to sell many products to the EU without paying tariffs. title: The missing votes
content: While EU citizens can move freely and settle anywhere within the Union, they cannot vote in national elections where they live, unless they are also citizens of that country. Though mobile EU citizens can vote in municipal elections and can also run for the European Parliament in their country of residence, an estimated 11.8 million of them have no say in national elections there. If mobile Europeans could vote, they'd likely have a significant influence on electoral outcomes in their host countries. One reason is that they tend to be younger than the local population, according to our analysis of data from Eurostat. Although mobile Europeans generally retain the right to vote in their country of citizenship, research and survey data consistently show that citizens living abroad vote less. Distance, bureaucratic hurdles, and a gradual disconnect from the politics of a country they no longer live in, all contribute to lower turnout. As a result, millions of mobile Europeans may be effectively falling out of democratic participation altogether.

title: The blood grain train rolling through the Baltics
content: Trainload after trainload of “blood grain” is crossing Latvia's eastern border. This is what locals are calling Russian grain, which has found a new route to the Baltic Sea after Ukrainian attacks disrupted the standard route through the Black Sea. Though many Latvians reject the idea of allowing Russian products that could help Moscow fund its war on Ukraine to pass through, the route is completely legal. The EU deliberately left Russian agriculture and food products out of its sanctions, arguing that restrictions could worsen global food security, particularly in developing countries. In 2024, the EU did set tariffs high enough to keep Russian grain off the European market, but made an exception for grain passing through on its way to other countries. Russia is one of the world's largest wheat exporters. Ukraine is making that grain machine sputter. In August, it struck Novorossiysk, Russia's main Black Sea port, knocking out three major grain terminals and disrupting crucial routes: last season, almost 90% of Russia's seaborne grain exports went through the Black Sea. title: Why the world thinks all Germans wear lederhosen
content: Oktoberfest is in full swing in Munich, running until Sunday 4 October. Last year, some 6.5 million people flocked to the festival, including a large share of international visitors (21%). The festival is known around the world, and Oktoberfest-style events have popped up everywhere, arguably making it the most famous German cultural export “product”. What most people don't know is that Oktoberfest is just one of thousands of regional Volksfeste (folk festivals) held across Germany throughout the year. And no, they're not just about beer. Beer tents are usually part of the deal, but so are fairground rides like carousels, Ferris wheels, and rollercoasters, along with travelling fairground businesses, market stalls, and other entertainment. Many began centuries ago as church fairs, agricultural celebrations, horse races, shooting festivals, or sailing regattas. title: Who pays for pricier carbon? You, until the help arrives
content: If you heat your home and fill up your car with gas, oil, or coal, your bills are likely going up from 2028. The EU’s new carbon pricing system, the Emissions Trading System 2 (ETS2), will make fossil fuel suppliers pay for the emissions from the fuel they sell, and they’ll pass that cost on to you. For most households, the increase in heating costs will be modest at around €60 a year on average, according to estimates from the Bertelsmann Foundation. But in Poland, households heating with oil, gas, or coal could pay €372 more each year. The hardest hit are often older homeowners in Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Poland, living on around half the average income in their countries. They already spend about 6% of their income on heating, and ETS2 could push that above 7%. Three in four buildings in the EU are energy inefficient, so they use more energy than necessary and every price rise costs them more. At an EU-wide renovation rate of around 1% a year, most won't be fixed any time soon. The EU is offering a safety net for the people hit hardest by ETS2: the Social Climate Fund. title: Estonia is crisis-proofing, and it starts in a gym
content: As far as (unofficial) national mottos go, “fortune favours the prepared” would be a fitting one for Estonia. After centuries of occupation and oppression, few countries seem to be as prepared for Russian aggression as Estonia. On a sunny day in June, this readiness was rehearsed in the town of Rapla, an hour south of Tallinn. In its main sports hall, Triinu Maandi and a handful of other women set up sleeping bags, bedding, and supplies for 350 people. Maandi and roughly 4,000 fellow volunteers of the Women’s Voluntary Defence Organisation would work alongside professional emergency responders in the event of a military conflict. “Given our history, it's a miracle that we can speak Estonian,” Maandi told us. “What came after Soviet [occupation] at the beginning of the 90s was a wreck. So we are trying to do what we can to prevent that from happening again.” Rapla’s sports hall is one of 340 evacuation sites across Estonia, with a combined capacity for approximately 70,000 people. title: Forgot what you walked into a room for? Blame the door
content: We've all experienced it: you walk into a room, and all of a sudden your mind goes blank. What on earth did you go in there to do? That annoying little brain fart has a name: the doorway effect. A new study in the journal Brain and Environment may have come one step closer to figuring out why it happens: when we move from one room to another, there’s an increase in theta activity in the brain. Theta waves are one of five types of brain waves, which are electrical currents measurable through electrodes on the scalp. “Many things in the brain are associated with this theta response,” co-author Zakaria Djebbara told us: memory, spatial awareness, and the brain’s map of the body, for example. Djebbara is an associate professor at Aalborg University in northern Denmark and researches how architecture affects the brain. “The reason we forget might be because the brain resets the understanding of the environment the moment we walk through the door,” Djebbara explained. In the study, electrodes measured the brain activity of 20 participants as they walked through virtual rooms. title: Good news for the planet, bad news for Norway
content: Norway has a green reputation, but it's one of the world's largest exporters of oil and gas, and the EU is its main customer. That could change: the EU is upholding a ban on new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, despite heavy lobbying from Oslo. Norway has become the Union’s largest gas supplier since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, providing roughly a third of its imports. Most of that gas comes from the North Sea, but some already flows from the Arctic, where Norway has produced gas since 2007 and opened its northernmost oil field last year. The country's production is forecast to decline after 2027 unless new reserves are found, most of which are expected in the northern Barents Sea. The EU would rather those reserves stay in the ground. In 2021, it committed to seeking an international moratorium on new Arctic oil and gas extraction, with backing from Germany, Sweden, and Finland. Norway recently lobbied hard for the EU to remove the ban from its upcoming revised Arctic strategy. Norway isn't in the EU, so the EU has no legal power over drilling in Norwegian waters. title: The how-to guide for turning nature into a border guard
content: It's called “The Game”. The perilous journey migrants take through the Balkans in the hope of reaching the European Union. The 931 kilometre-long border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and EU member state Croatia is one of its focal points. “This border runs across steep mountains, vast rivers, and through dense forests,” Tristan Solf of the Border Violence Monitoring Network (BVMN) told The European Correspondent (TEC). Its rugged landscape rivals that of the Białowieża Forest along the Poland-Belarus border and the Strandzha Mountains between Bulgaria and Turkey – both known for their dense, untamed terrain. As part of the Infranature Project, Solf studied how Croatian authorities use nature to deter migrants. By framing forests, rivers, and mountains as the source of danger, responsibility for deaths and disappearances can be shifted away from the border policies. “Outsourcing the border to nature only blurs accountability for the dangers the EU produces”, he said. title: Solarpunk could be the future we actually want
content: Morning light filters through houses draped in climbing plants. Rooftops hum with solar panels, and the air feels cooler in the shade of thousands of trees. This dream vision represents solarpunk. It imagines a future that pushes back against decades of dystopian climate narratives. The definition of solarpunk is evolving, but scholars tend to agree that it is positive, progressive and communal. You have probably already encountered it in your everyday life – in video games, music or advertising. Bits of it can be identified in science fiction series like Star Trek, anime like Castle in the Sky, or even Disney movies such as Tomorrowland. A real-life example is the residential Vertical Forest in Milan. You just didn't know it was solarpunk. Why (solar) punk? “Solar” refers to renewable energy. “Punk” signals how the movement challenges the status quo with utopian thinking. Solarpunk emerged in dialogue with the more conflictual genres of cyberpunk and steampunk. title: Berlin got hacked, and it shouldn't have been this easy
content: Headlines this month about Germany’s historic far-right win eclipsed another equally grim local record: nearly 6 terabytes of data from Berlin’s digital archives were leaked onto the dark web, in the country’s largest public administration hack to date. The files reportedly contain information on civil servants, private citizens and key infrastructure, including logins, contracts, payslips, medical records and ID copies. A full investigation is still underway, and authorities did not respond to our requests for comment at the time of publication. Whodunit? Rhysida, a notorious financially motivated ransomware team, claimed responsibility for the attack. Data collected by the extortion monitoring platform eCrime.ch and reviewed by The European Correspondent (TEC) links the group to 287 crimes in 39 countries, many of them targeting public administrations. Between 7 and 12 August, Rhysida allegedly infiltrated two Berlin government agencies. It used a phishing email containing a link to a fake CAPTCHA, a test that typically discerns human traffic from bots. title: AI is taking over ... the internet
content: The next time you see a typo in an online article or webpage, don't get annoyed – it might be a sign that an actual human wrote it. According to a recent analysis by the Pew Research Center, over one third of webpages published since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 were written with the help of AI. Using a random sample of 10,000 webpages, researchers concluded that 9.6% of all pages ever published show “significant signs of AI editing or authorship.” As LLMs have become widely available, writing has become cheap. Their output is rewriting a resource most of us rely on every day: the internet. Writing is difficult because it pushes you to think, which in turn helps to make up your mind. When we outsource that process to machines, and increasingly consume text produced by them, we risk losing out on our ability to think critically. But we're also surrendering our (potentially) greatest encyclopaedia of all time to non-human “thought” without quite knowing what comes after. At the risk of tooting our own horn, human-written journalism is one tool to keep this from happening. Typos andall.

title: The drone war never sleeps in Kyiv
content: For the past four years, Kyiv has lived by an unwritten rule of war: survive the night, and life can return to normal in the morning. That started to change at the end of August. Between 27 August and 1 September, Kyiv spent 60 hours under air-raid alerts, an unprecedented stretch since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Three weeks later, those days look less like an exceptionally bad week and more like the beginning of a new normal. This escalation marks a new development in Russia’s drone campaign. title: We can still refreeze the climate ice cube
content: “If you take an ice cube out of the freezer and put it on the table, it starts to melt. If you put the ice cube back in the freezer quick enough, it will freeze again,” climate scientist Nico Wunderling tells me. “But if you wait too long, it will melt entirely before you put it back, and you can’t put the water back into the cube form.” He’s explaining climate tipping points, his area of research at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Goethe University Frankfurt. Tipping points are thresholds where a small rise in warming triggers a self-reinforcing feedback loop that becomes very hard to reverse. Think of the melting Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets as giant versions of the melting ice cube. As ice sheets melt and shrink, their surfaces move into warmer air at lower elevations, causing them to melt even faster. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle: the more the ice melts, the warmer the air around it becomes, accelerating further melting. This commits them to near-total collapse over centuries, raising sea levels by metres. But these ice cubes can be refrozen, if they’re put back into the freezer fast enough. title: The EU's plan to childproof the internet
content: Last week, the European Commission unveiled its KIDS Act, a plan that would change how children under 15 interact with the internet across the EU. Over the past two years, nearly all member states have considered some form of age restriction on social platforms. The Commission’s proposal would override this potential patchwork of national laws with one EU-wide rule. This is not simply a social media ban, though. The proposal is much broader. It essentially regulates access to some digital services considered particularly “bad for children” while also requiring companies to make them safer by design. New rules for the new kids on the bloc The KIDS Act applies to seven types of platforms: social media, video-sharing, online games, app stores, operating systems, AI chatbots and AI companions – albeit in different ways. For social media and video-sharing platforms, the proposal creates an age ladder: no accounts under 13, “mini accounts” for 13- and 14-year-olds. These capped profiles would have to be set up by parents and come with a one-hour daily usage limit. Teens could then roam on a brand new, “safer-by-design” version of the internet. title: Protected on paper, burning in practice
content: In wildfire seasons between 2015 and 2025, protected nature around the size of Montenegro burned in Europe, according to The European Correspondent's analysis of data from the European Data Journalism Network. That's 1.3 million hectares, or almost 2% of Europe's protected areas under Natura 2000, a network of protected nature sites across the EU. These areas are disproportionately affected by wildfires. Though they only make up 18.6% of European land, around 29% of the area that has burned over the past 11 years was protected under Natura 2000. Portugal's on-land Natura 2000 areas were most affected, with 13% having burned at some point between 2015 and 2025. Over 3% of the area covered by Natura 2000 burned in Spain, Greece, and Hungary each. In August 2023, a 16-day-long megafire in Evros in northern Greece burned around 96,600 hectares of which 65% was part of a Natura 2000 area. In some cases, this land burns over and over. Around 23,200 hectares in the Danube Delta in Romania, protected because of its rare wetland habitats and vast biodiversity, have burned multiple times during five wildfire seasons. title: Climate disasters are expensive. Guess who's paying?
content: “Everything has burnt down. It was a big house on a lovely little plot. It had a swimming pool, and it’s burnt down,” a woman from Villa del Prado in Madrid said, in tears, to the Spanish public broadcaster in July. Her plot was devastated after the largest wildfire in Spain's history, which burnt 77,000 hectares. Almost two months later, there is still no official toll of the losses caused by the flames in central Spain, but the European Environment Agency (EEA) has estimated that the direct economic damage in the EU due to weather-related disasters reached €822 billion between 1980 and 2024. One quarter of this loss happened in the last four years. Floods were responsible for almost half of the total cost. “The climate related risks are real and their macroeconomic impact is increasing,” Georg Zachmann, senior fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, told The European Correspondent. The science is clear that extreme weather events will keep happening, he explained. title: Solar power with a side of strawberries
content: Nicolas Etchelecu will soon be taking over his parents' strawberry farm in the south of France. Their family business has transformed rapidly in the last couple of years. In 2022, they started building a new 3,000-sq-metre greenhouse with a roof made of solar panels: a first of its kind in France. These are “smart” panels: when built-in sensors detect too much sunlight, the panels close automatically to create shade and protect the strawberry plants from excessive heat. When the weather is favourable, and the plants need direct sun, the sensors open the shades. That way, the solar panels help protect the plants from extreme heatwaves, like the ones that hit France this summer, while generating clean electricity at the same time. This new approach to combining farming and solar power is called “agrivoltaics”. Across Europe, agri-panels could create the capacity of up to 51 TW – enough to generate 25 times more than the total current electricity demand in Europe. “The potential of this technology is almost unlimited,” Jiří Bím, a Czech agrivoltaics researcher, told The European Correspondent. title: Back to university, unless you're from Gaza
content: Salwa Abu Elhaj is 23 years old and lives in a tent in Gaza with her parents and siblings. Had everything gone to plan, she would now be at the KU Leuven campus to start her master's in communication science, for which she was awarded a scholarship. Salwa is one of a group of 13 students and researchers from Gaza with scholarships to study in Belgian universities in Antwerp, Brussels, Hasselt, and Leuven. None of them have appeared on campus so far. “I never imagined that I would have to fight this hard just to reach a university that had already accepted me,” Salwa told The European Correspondent. The federal government of Belgium hasn't helped the students apply for a visa in a Belgian consulate, nor has it been willing to organise a diplomatic evacuation. What's stopping them isn't the students' status or the logistics of leaving Gaza, but political bargaining over migration. Belgium's government couldn't reach an agreement on the issue. title: Going far right?
content: Support for far-right parties across Europe has increased in recent years. Added up across the continent, they won 23.5% of votes in the five countries that held parliamentary elections in 2025, and 23.2% in seven countries in 2026, according to PopuList, a peer-reviewed list of populist, far-right, far-left, and Eurosceptic parties. Support for these parties started taking off after 2015, increasing from around 5-6% in the 1990s. However, a few recent examples show that Europe is not moving in just one direction. Hungary and Poland, two former far-right strongholds, elected more moderate governments in their last elections. And the recent Swedish election delivered an upset too. Support for Sverigedemokraterna fell, dropping the far-right party to third place.

title: The fish skin that becomes one with your body
content: Guðmundur Fertram Sigurjónsson, an inventor and CEO originally from a small Icelandic fishing village, was looking at fish scales for wound healing, and realised fish skin is structurally similar to human skin. And this makes it an interesting alternative for dressing wounds. Unlike conventional wound dressings – which need to be replaced, potentially damaging fragile new tissue – North Atlantic cod skin stays on the wound. The body's cells grow into it, and as new human tissue develops, the cod skin is gradually absorbed and replaced by the patient's own living tissue. Humans have used animal skin to cover wounds since as far back as the 16th century. Pigs became the dominant donor in modern medicine, largely for their affordability as well as their similarity to human skin. But while mammal skin needs to undergo harsh treatment to eliminate the risk of disease transmission, cod skin may carry little risk of spreading disease to humans, since certain pathogens adapted to cold-water fish struggle to survive in the warmer human body, Sigurjónsson explained to us. title: Mind the tone
content: People are notoriously bad at picking up spoken words when caught off-guard, especially in a noisy, crowded train. Passengers with visual impairments need special attention too. A few musical notes work like a familiar tap on the shoulder, prompting our brains to listen. Designing these little jingles is a delicate exercise: the melody needs to cut through the hum of engines and screech of wheels without startling commuters. The jingles must rely on moderately fast “attacks” (that regulate how quickly a sound reaches full volume), sustained “pulse rates” (the speed and spacing between notes), and a range of musical patterns, sometimes ascending, some descending, and others using a back-and-forth sequence. But they must also be pleasant to our ears. content: “If Europe were to prepare for the Second World War with today's tenders and procedures, then D-Day would happen not in 1944 but in 1951,” Leo Litra, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told us, referencing research from his ECFR colleagues. title: Sweden (barely) beats the far-right
content: What happened: The Social Democrat-led centre-left opposition very narrowly won parliamentary elections in Sweden, defeating the ruling right-wing minority government, which was supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats. There is a three seat difference between the two blocs. It was so close that counting continued until Wednesday – with a margin of around 27,000 votes. Why this matters: Besides giving Europe's battered centre-left – after a string of electoral losses across the continent – a much-needed victory, the result also offers Europe a lesson: there appears to be a limit to how far voters are willing to accept increasingly restrictive migration policy. title: From Finland to Portugal by train in just 125 hours
content: Last week, Jon Worth, a railway activist who advocates for better cross-border train travel across Europe, completed the longest train journey in the EU – from Kemijärvi in northern Finland to Lagos in southern Portugal – in a speedy 125 hours and 31 minutes. title: Why is Britain going crazy over a medieval embroidery?
content: The Bayeux Tapestry has been on display at the British Museum since 10 September, and everyone in Britain wants to see it. In July, 80,000 people joined the online queue at its peak – some waiting up to nine hours – to get tickets. content: What happened: Yesterday (15 September), the European Commission promised to cut some of the annoying paperwork that makes it harder for EU workers to move to another country. Social security and health insurance documents, as well as diplomas, would also be available via European digital identity wallets, free mobile apps that store verified personal identification documents. Member states are required to make them a reality across the EU by the end of this year. title: What makes Europe strong?
content: Across the EU, priorities for strengthening Europe's global standing have consolidated. In spring 2024, defence, energy independence, or competitiveness were already the top priorities in 20 of the EU's 27 member states. By spring 2026, that had risen to 25 of 27, while climate action and food security faded as leading concerns. In 2026, Spain and Sweden are the only exceptions: Spain puts education and research first, while Sweden prioritises democratic values.

title: Human rights, but optional
content: On 13 September, Turkish police cracked down on people, bars, and rights groups associated with the LGBTQ+ community. Under the guise of protecting family values, they arrested dozens, including 50 activists from the rights group Kaos GL alone. Kaos GL previously won a legal case at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) against the Turkish government for another crackdown in 2017. The ECtHR was created to protect the fundamental human rights set out in the European Convention on Human Rights, a post-World War II treaty with 46 European members. It's overseen by the Council of Europe, a separate institution from the EU. When the ECtHR finds that a violation has occurred, its judgment is legally binding, meaning the country is required to comply with it. Yet almost a decade after the judgment in favour of Kaos GL, the Turkish government's attack against LGBTQ+ people has only intensified. In a different case from 2019, the ECtHR ruled Türkiye should release prominent philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala. The Turkish government didn't comply. title: If you're reading this, you're in the minority
content: In the winter of 2015, Canadian rapper Drake released a mixtape with the plainest cover I'd ever seen: seven words hand-lettered in black on plain white: If You're Reading This It's Too Late. That same year, a non-profit called OpenAI was founded in San Francisco. Nobody linked the two moments. Why would they? Well, seven years later, OpenAI released ChatGPT, and the web hasn't been the same since. AI flooded the space we had spent decades building for each other, one post, one blog, and one comment at a time. The numbers are clear. Stack Overflow was once the beating, chaotic heart of programmer culture, where strangers helped strangers debug their code at 2am. Its monthly questions have collapsed from 109,152 in November 2022, the month ChatGPT launched, to 1,146 in August 2026. Social media users complain, louder every month, about feeds drowning in AI slop: generic, soulless images and captions built to be scrolled past, not actually read or felt. title: Couldn't think straight this summer? Same
content: You wake up on a hot morning. You're sweating, and you haven't slept well. Your head aches, the workday ahead makes you anxious, and the birds chirping outside make you want to scream. If you lived through this summer's heatwaves in Europe, you know this is hardly an exaggeration of what a typical day can feel like. Record temperatures had Europeans feeling frustrated and dizzy. Part of the reason has to do with how our brain works. Our brain makes up only 2% of our body mass, but eats up 20% of our energy. During a heatwave or short exposure to extremely high temperatures, the heart struggles to keep everything cool. “The heart has to pump blood to the periphery of the body to help the body sweat, and for that it has to work hard. When heat exceeds our capacity to sweat, the supply of blood to the brain might not be optimal anymore, and the brain starts to overheat,” said Pieter Vancamp, a neurobiologist at the PhanLab in Nantes, France. You might not notice the difference between 30°C and 31°C, but your brain does: even a shift of less than a degree alters our nervous system. title: Eating our way through the city, for free
content: Growing up, I used to walk around the allotments – those small city gardens – to see if any vegetables or fruit hanging over the fence could be put into my belly. I revisited that habit recently, snacking on yellow plums that had begun transforming into jam on the pavement (I went for the ones still round but perfectly ripe). Some gardeners volunteer their harvest, putting apples in boxes on the streets with a little sign saying to “take some”. Urban foraging is hardly new, although collaborative maps and edible-city projects have made it far more visible. Falling Fruit is one such map. Launched in 2013, it shows where there's food up for grabs in cities across the globe. I looked up the closest edible location to me in Brussels on the map – it was a Carrefour dumpster, with a little comment in French: “Some Monday or Thursday evenings, a black container containing bread and sometimes other items.” Alright, how about something offering a more classic foraging experience? There – a pear tree, 37 minutes away on foot. title: Autumn foliage
content: Summer is over and autumn is upon us! While Europe may not have the spectacular autumn landscapes of North America, it offers a smaller but more varied seasonal display. The timing of autumn senescence – the changing colour and falling of leaves – varies widely across the continent. In southern Europe, colours can appear as early as late August, while in central and northern Europe, trees often stay green well into October or even November before changing and shedding their leaves. This visualisation was first published in September 2025.
